Given a query and a passage, you must provide a score on an integer scale of 0 to 3 with the following meanings:
0 = represent that the passage has nothing to do with the query, 
1 = represents that the passage seems related to the query but does not answer it, 
2 = represents that the passage has some answer for the query, but the answer may be a bit unclear, or hidden amongst extraneous information and 
3 = represents that the passage is dedicated to the query and contains the exact answer.

Important Instruction: Assign category 1 if the passage is somewhat related to the topic but not completely, category 2 if passage presents something very important related to the entire topic but also has some extra information and category 3 if the passage only and entirely refers to the topic. If none of the above satisfies give it category 0.

Query: I am a software engineer at a small startup, trying to scale our product to around 1M users / day from around the world. The service is a social media app similar to twitter, where users can write a message and follow others. Right now we have a simple web interface with a local mySQL database. Please write a technical report on the transition to more scaled software and provide recommendations for anything you consider a necessary change.
Passage: 1

2

And welcome to Punkspider and IOStation,
3

making a mess all over the internet.
4

I am Jason Hopper,
5

8

I'm the Director of Computer
Network Exploitation at QOMPLX.
9

- Years ago, Alex invented or developed
10

you know, how they're going

19

- Yeah, so start off with
a little history lesson
20
00:00:44,830 --> 00:00:47,880
on what the fuck is PunkSPIDER, right?
21
00:00:47,880 --> 00:00:51,830
So PunkSPIDER was a distributed
math web application

fuzzing project run over a Hadoop cluster

what the fuck that means

that's usually how people remember it.

So if you remember something like that,

that was QOMPLX.

It was presented at ShmooCon on 2013,

at the DEFCON 2014 as well, so.
37

Still a long time ago
during this old release,

If you remember that time

then you remember times

So what we'd love people

We had an open API,

That was old chip, old technology,

good stuff that inspired

money, backing,

legitimacy,

everything possible for us
to succeed in this project.
108
00:04:37,620 --> 00:04:41,950
Meaning that really, this
thing is flying right now.

00:04:41,950 --> 00:04:43,730
And I'll get into some of the numbers

00:04:43,730 --> 00:04:45,180
and we'll get into some of the specifics

00:04:45,180 --> 00:04:48,330
of what we're checking for
in PunkSPIDER right now.

00:04:48,330 --> 00:04:49,940
But this thing is really flying.

It's got dedicated engineering time.

It's not going back down, put it that way,

and it's only gonna get better and better.
116
00:04:56,550 --> 00:04:59,660
But anyway, that's

117

Hopper here is gonna give you

some bit of backstory about IOStation.
119
00:05:03,350 --> 00:05:07,350
- Yeah, so IOStation used
to be called Omnisense.
120
00:05:07,350 --> 00:05:11,490
I apologize if I accidentally
say that in a sentence later,
121
00:05:11,490 --> 00:05:15,650
but Sysadmins have similarly
never liked this program
122
00:05:15,650 --> 00:05:17,250
or the system either.
123
00:05:17,250 --> 00:05:19,130
It started pretty innocently, and sorry,
124
00:05:19,130 --> 00:05:22,057
what it is is just a giant
collection of tools that generate
125
00:05:22,057 --> 00:05:25,720
and aggregate data and make
that available to a user.
126
00:05:25,720 --> 00:05:27,940
And it really did start
out quite innocently.
127
00:05:27,940 --> 00:05:29,830
I was just coming into
the cybersecurity space
128
00:05:29,830 --> 00:05:32,780
and I started learning
about just how crazy
129
00:05:32,780 --> 00:05:35,360
the DNS system is.
130
00:05:35,360 --> 00:05:36,360
Like what you can do with it,
131
00:05:36,360 --> 00:05:37,910
the way that it's exploited
132
00:05:37,910 --> 00:05:39,620
and it's such a seemingly simple system,
133
00:05:39,620 --> 00:05:42,090
but I couldn't believe
the, like the depth.
134
00:05:42,090 --> 00:05:42,990
And I was, you know,
135
00:05:42,990 --> 00:05:45,950
learning about DNS amplification
attacks and decided,
136
00:05:45,950 --> 00:05:47,350
because the way that I learned things best
137
00:05:47,350 --> 00:05:48,450
is by recreating the wheel,
138
00:05:48,450 --> 00:05:51,260
that I would just write a
DNS server from scratch,
139
00:05:51,260 --> 00:05:53,980
and I turned it into an
amplification sinkhole
140
00:05:53,980 --> 00:05:55,750
and then started just getting
real interested in that.
141
00:05:55,750 --> 00:05:57,610
So I was writing a blog post
142
00:05:57,610 --> 00:05:59,100
and I wanted to say, there are, you know,
143
00:05:59,100 --> 00:06:02,630
this many open recursive
DNS servers on the internet.
144
00:06:02,630 --> 00:06:03,930
Recursive DNS server, of course,
145
00:06:03,930 --> 00:06:06,810
being one that will answer
a query for any domain,
146
00:06:06,810 --> 00:06:09,060
it'll go out and find
the answer up the tree.
147
00:06:10,060 --> 00:06:10,893
And so I started,
148
00:06:10,893 --> 00:06:11,870
I couldn't find that answer,
149
00:06:11,870 --> 00:06:12,850
how many there were on the internet?
150
00:06:12,850 --> 00:06:15,920
So I started writing a little
Python script to do the scan,
151
00:06:15,920 --> 00:06:16,753
to find them.
152
00:06:16,753 --> 00:06:19,160
And then, you know, I realized that,
153
00:06:19,160 --> 00:06:21,740
although that sounds simple
and conceptually it's simple,
154
00:06:21,740 --> 00:06:23,380
there really is a lot of
subtleties to actually
155
00:06:23,380 --> 00:06:26,260
being able to do even
a simple scan at scale.
156
00:06:26,260 --> 00:06:28,320
And, you know, and then,
and then, and then,
157
00:06:28,320 --> 00:06:30,290
it's some giant deep rabbit hole.
158
00:06:30,290 --> 00:06:31,623
And before I knew it,
159
00:06:32,600 --> 00:06:34,200
you know, I had this big system.
160
00:06:35,270 --> 00:06:37,330
It's made up of many different parts,
161
00:06:37,330 --> 00:06:39,510
but the primary parts are port scanning.
162
00:06:39,510 --> 00:06:42,570
It's scanning over 25 ports.
163
00:06:42,570 --> 00:06:45,730
There's a lot of like custom
extractions that it's doing.
164
00:06:45,730 --> 00:06:47,830
In addition to the obvious
stuff like banner grabbing
165
00:06:47,830 --> 00:06:50,033
and service detection
and things like that.
166
00:06:51,090 --> 00:06:51,923
On the Darkweb,
167
00:06:51,923 --> 00:06:53,750
we're again doing port scanning,
168
00:06:53,750 --> 00:06:56,030
we're trying to tease out any information
169
00:06:56,030 --> 00:06:58,400
on additional onion sites
that might be hosted
170
00:06:58,400 --> 00:06:59,233
on the same VM
171
00:06:59,233 --> 00:07:01,270
or definitely any way that we can link it
172
00:07:01,270 --> 00:07:04,010
to a surface IP address or
domain or something like that
173
00:07:04,010 --> 00:07:05,870
to do any attribution
for sites that, you know,
174
00:07:05,870 --> 00:07:08,273
should be taken down with
from law enforcement.
175
00:07:09,470 --> 00:07:11,580
We're also, of course, crawling
all these websites as well.
176
00:07:11,580 --> 00:07:15,540
So we're doing, you know,
Darkweb mentions for, you know,
177
00:07:15,540 --> 00:07:18,220
corporate entities and names
of other things of interest.
178
00:07:18,220 --> 00:07:21,800
And, you know, coming from
the pure cybersecurity space
179
00:07:21,800 --> 00:07:22,633
when we joined QOMPLX.
180
00:07:22,633 --> 00:07:24,760
QOMPLX is a cybersecurity company,
181
00:07:24,760 --> 00:07:27,880
but they really focus in assessing risk
182
00:07:27,880 --> 00:07:29,430
and transforming risk.
183
00:07:29,430 --> 00:07:31,150
And so there's a bit of a mind shift
184
00:07:31,150 --> 00:07:32,310
that had to happen on my part
185
00:07:32,310 --> 00:07:34,270
where some things that are really good
186
00:07:34,270 --> 00:07:37,330
for pure cybersecurity actually
don't inform risk that well,
187
00:07:37,330 --> 00:07:39,360
and there are a lot of other tools
188
00:07:39,360 --> 00:07:40,450
that you can use in its place.
189
00:07:40,450 --> 00:07:43,090
So I've sort of been
working on the system,
190
00:07:43,090 --> 00:07:44,660
but with that very much in mind.
191
00:07:44,660 --> 00:07:46,930
So a lot of the new kind
of directions that I'm,
192
00:07:46,930 --> 00:07:47,763
or the new tooling
193
00:07:47,763 --> 00:07:49,020
or the new things that I'm interested in
194
00:07:49,020 --> 00:07:51,190
really are kind of going
down that namespace,
195
00:07:51,190 --> 00:07:53,940
and that can be simple things
or seemingly simple things
196
00:07:53,940 --> 00:07:56,660
like even just identifying
what a corporation has.
197
00:07:56,660 --> 00:07:57,570
Like what are their assets?
198
00:07:57,570 --> 00:07:58,680
Where are they?
199
00:07:58,680 --> 00:07:59,810
Some corporations, honestly,
200
00:07:59,810 --> 00:08:02,310
can't even answer that question for you.
201
00:08:02,310 --> 00:08:05,140
And so doing this in a kind
of broad autonomous fashion
202
00:08:05,140 --> 00:08:06,610
is really interesting.
203
00:08:06,610 --> 00:08:08,450
How that informs other
sort of risk metrics
204
00:08:08,450 --> 00:08:10,120
and then looking at
kind of proxy measures,
205
00:08:10,120 --> 00:08:12,050
like what jobs are they hiring?
206
00:08:12,050 --> 00:08:13,810
What technologies do they
have in those job ads?
207
00:08:13,810 --> 00:08:16,260
Like how does that
potentially inform, you know,
208
00:08:16,260 --> 00:08:18,440
what they're doing in-house?
209
00:08:18,440 --> 00:08:20,040
We also have some passive sensors,
210
00:08:20,040 --> 00:08:21,130
so I'll call them, you know,
211
00:08:21,130 --> 00:08:23,900
we're monitoring the global
certificate transparency logs.
212
00:08:23,900 --> 00:08:26,530
So pretty well, any SSL
certificate that's generated,
213
00:08:26,530 --> 00:08:29,710
we record a copy of in near real-time.
214
00:08:29,710 --> 00:08:32,660
And then we also have another
significant component,
215
00:08:32,660 --> 00:08:33,870
which is our listening network.
216
00:08:33,870 --> 00:08:36,730
So they're basically these
low interaction honeypots
217
00:08:36,730 --> 00:08:38,060
that are distributed globally
218
00:08:38,060 --> 00:08:40,270
and all across the IPv4 spectrum.
219
00:08:40,270 --> 00:08:44,500
And they're out there sort
of just, you know, listening.
220
00:08:44,500 --> 00:08:47,310
They then can identify the early onset
221
00:08:47,310 --> 00:08:49,510
of any sort of broad malicious activity
222
00:08:49,510 --> 00:08:51,500
or benign activity for that matter.
223
00:08:51,500 --> 00:08:54,420
And we can use that as a
way to profile the threat
224
00:08:54,420 --> 00:08:56,630
in like a socklog, for example, you know,
225
00:08:56,630 --> 00:08:58,410
socks have a lot to deal with.
226
00:08:58,410 --> 00:08:59,990
They don't need to be chasing
down leads that ended up
227
00:08:59,990 --> 00:09:01,220
just being like Google crawlers
228
00:09:01,220 --> 00:09:04,203
or the university of, you
know, whatever doing research.
229
00:09:05,270 --> 00:09:08,370
Similarly, we can use this
to inform a risk score
230
00:09:08,370 --> 00:09:10,290
by looking at for any given corporation.
231
00:09:10,290 --> 00:09:12,000
If we know what our assets are,
232
00:09:12,000 --> 00:09:13,610
have any of them been involved in say,
233
00:09:13,610 --> 00:09:14,800
being part of a botnet?
234
00:09:14,800 --> 00:09:16,070
And if so, for how long?
235
00:09:16,070 --> 00:09:17,940
Like, you know, getting popped,
236
00:09:17,940 --> 00:09:19,830
you know, once last year is one thing.
237
00:09:19,830 --> 00:09:23,150
Getting popped and then
remaining part of botnet
238
00:09:23,150 --> 00:09:26,100
or whatever for six months
is kind of something else,
239
00:09:26,100 --> 00:09:28,070
that sort of speaks to their detection
240
00:09:28,070 --> 00:09:29,860
and remediation policies.
241
00:09:29,860 --> 00:09:32,020
Of course, I still have the
amplification attack sinkhole.
242
00:09:32,020 --> 00:09:34,720
It's not the most
particularly valuable sensor,
243
00:09:34,720 --> 00:09:37,038
but you know, it's an oldie and a goodie.
244
00:09:37,038 --> 00:09:38,010
And then you know, honestly,
245
00:09:38,010 --> 00:09:39,690
I started learning that if you
246
00:09:39,690 --> 00:09:41,170
just start registering with places
247
00:09:41,170 --> 00:09:42,630
and then looking under some rocks,
248

00:39:18,680 --> 00:39:21,010
but Mozi.a, it executes
it slightly differently.
1067
00:39:21,010 --> 00:39:23,800
But basically this looks
like it's trying to do this
1068
00:39:23,800 --> 00:39:25,710
on netgear equipment at a minimum.
1069
00:39:25,710 --> 00:39:29,170
And we know from PunkSPIDER
that there are tons of websites
1070
00:39:29,170 --> 00:39:32,040
that are vulnerable to
injection like this, so.
1071
00:39:32,040 --> 00:39:33,320
So I started digging a little bit deeper
1072
00:39:33,320 --> 00:39:36,030
and I used to listening, sorry,
1073
00:39:36,030 --> 00:39:37,690
I use this data to identify
1074
00:39:37,690 --> 00:39:39,520
where the attacks were coming from
1075
00:39:39,520 --> 00:39:41,350
and where the malware was being hosted.
1076
00:39:41,350 --> 00:39:42,328
And interestingly,
1077
00:39:42,328 --> 00:39:44,042
they were always different IP addresses,
1078
00:39:44,042 --> 00:39:45,930
whatever service, or sorry,
1079
00:39:45,930 --> 00:39:48,650
whatever computer was saying,
1080
00:39:48,650 --> 00:39:50,000
go download and run those malware
1081
00:39:50,000 --> 00:39:52,860
was never the same IP addresses
where it was being hosted.
1082
00:39:52,860 --> 00:39:55,530
And they were mainly hosted
in China, like predominantly,
1083
00:39:55,530 --> 00:39:56,760
you know, definitely some in India.
1084
00:39:56,760 --> 00:39:57,890
And of course it's a botnet,
1085
00:39:57,890 --> 00:39:59,640
so it's spread across the world.
1086
00:39:59,640 --> 00:40:02,450
But there was a huge amount
of it coming from China,
1087
00:40:02,450 --> 00:40:03,283
which was interesting
1088
00:40:03,283 --> 00:40:05,760
because then when I looked at what sensors
1089
00:40:05,760 --> 00:40:08,280
is the botnet was hitting mostly?
1090
00:40:08,280 --> 00:40:12,780
It was really heavily hitting
India, Japan, Australia,
1091
00:40:12,780 --> 00:40:14,820
and then to a slightly lesser degree,
1092
00:40:14,820 --> 00:40:16,150
Canada and Germany,
1093
00:40:16,150 --> 00:40:17,460
but there were no hits in China,
1094
00:40:17,460 --> 00:40:18,300
which was kind of funny.
1095
00:40:18,300 --> 00:40:19,790
And I'm not trying to suggest
that this is some sort of
1096
00:40:19,790 --> 00:40:23,770
like, you know, clever state
sponsored piece of malware
1097
00:40:23,770 --> 00:40:25,050
or anything like that.
1098
00:40:25,050 --> 00:40:25,883
I just thought it was funny
1099
00:40:25,883 --> 00:40:28,100
that none of my Chinese servers
actually saw any of this
1100
00:40:28,100 --> 00:40:30,010
and it almost looks like
kind of a geopolitical map,
1101
00:40:30,010 --> 00:40:32,080
you know, a little bit.
1102
00:40:32,080 --> 00:40:35,253
So yeah, China's
suspiciously missing there.
1103
00:40:36,570 --> 00:40:38,150
You know, I did dig in to look at
1104
00:40:38,150 --> 00:40:40,030
what devices were actually
being part of this botnet,
1105
00:40:40,030 --> 00:40:42,420
and it definitely look a
lot of D-Link, Netgear,
1106
00:40:42,420 --> 00:40:43,890
and Huawei gear.
1107
00:40:43,890 --> 00:40:45,470
I saw IPCameras, DVRs.
1108
00:40:45,470 --> 00:40:46,832
There were some GPON devices,
1109
00:40:46,832 --> 00:40:48,690
which was a little interesting.
1110
00:40:48,690 --> 00:40:50,440
I didn't really see
anything that indicated
1111
00:40:50,440 --> 00:40:52,410
it was part of any sort of
like corporate structure
1112
00:40:52,410 --> 00:40:53,243
or anything.
1113
00:40:53,243 --> 00:40:56,050
But the software being used
are a lot of web servers,
1114
00:40:56,050 --> 00:40:58,030
but they're all like kind
of small lightweight ones
1115
00:40:58,030 --> 00:41:00,260
that you see being used in
sort of embedded devices
1116
00:41:00,260 --> 00:41:01,093
and things like that,
1117
00:41:01,093 --> 00:41:02,250
like home routers.
1118
00:41:02,250 --> 00:41:07,250
And I did notice that the
lighttpd version that I saw,
1119
00:41:07,700 --> 00:41:11,320
a lot of actually 1.4.39
had just a ton of CVEs
1120
00:41:11,320 --> 00:41:13,420
and many of them were just like blanket,
1121
00:41:13,420 --> 00:41:15,490
you know, remote code execution
vulnerabilities and stuff,
1122
00:41:15,490 --> 00:41:17,200
which was kind of cool.
1123
00:41:17,200 --> 00:41:18,920
So I did kind of poke around
at a few of these things,
1124
00:41:18,920 --> 00:41:19,800
like what they were showing,
1125
00:41:19,800 --> 00:41:21,870
and I found this kind of cool example.
1126
00:41:21,870 --> 00:41:23,750
This was just somebody part of the botnet.
1127
00:41:23,750 --> 00:41:27,240
It has an interface that
looks a lot like dealing.
1128
00:41:27,240 --> 00:41:28,810
I didn't try to login
or anything like that.
1129
00:41:28,810 --> 00:41:31,130
The links on the top made you login,
1130
00:41:31,130 --> 00:41:32,740
but I did dig around the JavaScript
1131
00:41:32,740 --> 00:41:34,150
'cause it really wasn't
that much actually.
1132
00:41:34,150 --> 00:41:36,870
And I saw that it was
crafting these links,
1133
00:41:36,870 --> 00:41:38,440
so I went to a few of them directly
1134
00:41:38,440 --> 00:41:41,250
like a sys status.asp, for example.
1135
00:41:41,250 --> 00:41:44,010
And, you know, I guess it
doesn't always want you to login.
1136
00:41:44,010 --> 00:41:46,370
So if you go to them directly
at the login page actually,
1137
00:41:46,370 --> 00:41:48,290
works, or sorry, is bypassed.
1138
00:41:48,290 --> 00:41:50,790
And I was able to see all
the internal DHB tables,
1139
00:41:50,790 --> 00:41:53,060
and all the routing
information and all that stuff.
1140
00:41:53,060 --> 00:41:55,430
And, you know, while this
isn't some, you know,
1141
00:41:55,430 --> 00:41:58,260
egregious vulnerability
necessarily on its own right.
1142
00:41:58,260 --> 00:41:59,860
It's just kind of illustrating like,
1143
00:41:59,860 --> 00:42:00,850
this is the kind of nonsense
1144
00:42:00,850 --> 00:42:02,640
that is still all over the internet.
1145
00:42:02,640 --> 00:42:04,300
Like I know security has been a hot topic.
1146
00:42:04,300 --> 00:42:06,610
It's getting better, I think,
1147
00:42:06,610 --> 00:42:08,370
I think, anyway.
1148
00:42:08,370 --> 00:42:09,950
But there's still craziness like this,
1149
00:42:09,950 --> 00:42:13,520
where this person's router
just like lets you login,
1150
00:42:13,520 --> 00:42:15,900
and yeah, that's kind of crazy to me.
1151
00:42:15,900 --> 00:42:18,470
So, you know, we're kind of
running out of time here,
1152
00:42:18,470 --> 00:42:21,030
but I'm sure the burning
question in everyone's mind is
1153
00:42:21,030 --> 00:42:22,010
where's this all going?
1154
00:42:22,010 --> 00:42:23,920
So where where's it going, Alex?
1155
00:42:23,920 --> 00:42:24,753
- Right.
1156
00:42:24,753 --> 00:42:26,000
So I just want to recap
for everybody, right?
1157
00:42:26,000 --> 00:42:28,210
So a couple of quick things.
1158
00:42:28,210 --> 00:42:29,800
Created a hugely scalable system
1159
00:42:29,800 --> 00:42:31,790
for fuzzing a fuckton of URLs.
1160
00:42:31,790 --> 00:42:34,660
We've had a bunch of
vulnerabilities in major websites.
1161
00:42:34,660 --> 00:42:36,000
We've even found zero days
1162
00:42:36,000 --> 00:42:38,120
in a popular forum technology, right?
1163
00:42:38,120 --> 00:42:43,120
So obviously, the probably
most important part of that
1164
00:42:43,350 --> 00:42:45,300
is that we're releasing
that out to you all,
1165
00:42:45,300 --> 00:42:46,133
the public.
1166
00:42:47,090 --> 00:42:50,540
And we want to keep these results updated
1167
00:42:50,540 --> 00:42:52,810
while still continuing
to go extremely broad.
1168
00:42:52,810 --> 00:42:55,510
Our target is still the entire internet.
1169
00:42:55,510 --> 00:42:57,660
We're not gonna let down on that target.
1170
00:42:57,660 --> 00:42:59,410
We're gonna continue engineering
1171
00:42:59,410 --> 00:43:00,720
until we've reached that target
1172
00:43:00,720 --> 00:43:03,500
and we can keep the
records reasonably updated
1173
00:43:03,500 --> 00:43:05,230
to a certain degree, right?
1174
00:43:05,230 --> 00:43:07,940
So how can you kind of help us, right?
1175
00:43:07,940 --> 00:43:09,830
So I mentioned throwing us ideas,
1176
00:43:09,830 --> 00:43:11,640
obviously, it's is really helpful,
1177
00:43:11,640 --> 00:43:13,240
but download that extension.
1178
00:43:13,240 --> 00:43:17,173
Use that CLI tool, start
calling out websites,
1179
00:43:18,768 --> 00:43:22,370
all of these things are really helpful
1180
00:43:22,370 --> 00:43:23,840
and not only at the PunkSPIDER,
1181
00:43:23,840 --> 00:43:26,870
but part of the mission
of PunkSPIDER, really.
1182
00:43:26,870 --> 00:43:28,223
We built this for you all.
1183
00:43:31,503 --> 00:43:33,503
So feel pretty use it basically, is all.
1184
00:43:34,920 --> 00:43:36,810
- As far as IOStation is concerned,
1185
00:43:36,810 --> 00:43:40,790
you know, I think that
continuing to transform
1186
00:43:40,790 --> 00:43:45,170
my mindset from pure
cybersecurity to evaluating risk
1187
00:43:45,170 --> 00:43:46,850
and risk scoring is really interesting.
1188
00:43:46,850 --> 00:43:48,880
So I wanna continue kind
of going down that path.
1189
00:43:48,880 --> 00:43:51,010
That's not to say that there
won't still be the broad
1190
00:43:51,010 --> 00:43:53,360
internet collection tools
that have been working with
1191
00:43:53,360 --> 00:43:55,080
and know and love,
1192
00:43:55,080 --> 00:43:57,270
but it's just that some
of the newer features
1193
00:43:57,270 --> 00:43:59,890
that are coming out probably
will be geared towards that.
1194
00:43:59,890 --> 00:44:01,870
Especially when it comes
to critical infrastructure
1195
00:44:01,870 --> 00:44:03,190
and industrial control systems,
1196
00:44:03,190 --> 00:44:05,190
which for anyone paying
attention to the news lately,
1197
00:44:05,190 --> 00:44:07,590
I'm sure knows has been a
bit of a hot button topic
1198
00:44:07,590 --> 00:44:08,910
when it comes to certain pipelines,
1199
00:44:08,910 --> 00:44:09,953
which may not be named.
1200
00:44:09,953 --> 00:44:11,210
(laughs)
1201
00:44:11,210 --> 00:44:13,470
But I think that's a
really fascinating area,
1202
00:44:13,470 --> 00:44:15,120
and especially one that's, you know,
1203
00:44:15,120 --> 00:44:17,453
obviously, increasing importance.
1204
00:44:18,600 --> 00:44:20,290
I know there's a lot of utilities
1205
00:44:20,290 --> 00:44:21,610
and things that have really ignored
1206
00:44:21,610 --> 00:44:23,010
their cybersecurity posture,
1207
00:44:23,993 --> 00:44:25,670
and they're starting to get bit by it.
1208
00:44:25,670 --> 00:44:28,510
And anyways, that's something
I think we need to look at.
1209
00:44:28,510 --> 00:44:31,240
And the other one is a
little bit more vague,
1210
00:44:31,240 --> 00:44:34,210
but really trying to identify
attacker infrastructure.
1211
00:44:34,210 --> 00:44:36,150
Like are there things
that we can be observing
1212
00:44:36,150 --> 00:44:37,232
from the outside
1213
00:44:37,232 --> 00:44:41,120
to identify what an attacker is using
1214
00:44:41,120 --> 00:44:42,160
and how they're organizing?
1215
00:44:42,160 --> 00:44:45,250
But you know, maybe early
or on the onset or whatever,
1216
00:44:45,250 --> 00:44:47,210
as early as possible obviously is better.
1217
00:44:47,210 --> 00:44:50,860
You know, is there
software that can be probed
1218
00:44:50,860 --> 00:44:53,330
and identified running
across the internet?
1219
00:44:53,330 --> 00:44:56,960
Are there any sort of particular
techniques or patterns
1220
00:44:56,960 --> 00:44:59,190
or signatures or anything
like that that we can extract?
1221
00:44:59,190 --> 00:45:01,310
You know, this one is
not as well thought out.
1222
00:45:01,310 --> 00:45:02,870
Obviously, it's just something that
1223
00:45:02,870 --> 00:45:05,640
I think we're pretty interested
in tracking down long-term,
1224
00:45:05,640 --> 00:45:08,260
but I think that about wraps it up for us.
1225
00:45:08,260 --> 00:45:09,900
So yeah, if you want to shoot us an email
1226
00:45:09,900 --> 00:45:11,640
or whatever, feel free.
1227
00:45:11,640 --> 00:45:14,100
You can, you know, visit our office,
1228
00:45:14,100 --> 00:45:15,846
but Alex and I won't be there, so.
1229
00:45:15,846 --> 00:45:18,210
(laughs)
1230
00:45:18,210 --> 00:45:19,350
- Yeah.
1231
00:45:19,350 --> 00:45:20,910
Thanks everybody for coming in,
1232
00:45:20,910 --> 00:45:22,250
and listening to our talk.
1233
00:45:22,250 --> 00:45:23,530
We really appreciate it.
1234
00:45:23,530 --> 00:45:26,880
And, you know, thank you
all for taking the time
1235
00:45:26,880 --> 00:45:29,520
to listen us, ramble on about the system,
1236
00:45:29,520 --> 00:45:31,770
and I hope you really enjoyed it.
1237
00:45:31,770 --> 00:45:32,730
- Yeah, thanks everyone.
1238
00:45:32,730 --> 00:45:34,030
Take it easy. Bye bye.
1239
00:45:34,030 --> 00:45:35,280
- Peace everybody. Later.

Query: I am a software engineer at a small startup, trying to scale our product to around 1M users / day from around the world. The service is a social media app similar to twitter, where users can write a message and follow others. Right now we have a simple web interface with a local mySQL database. Please write a technical report on the transition to more scaled software and provide recommendations for anything you consider a necessary change.
Passage: 1
00:00:01,970 --> 00:00:02,803
- Hello, everyone.
2
00:00:02,803 --> 00:00:04,380
And welcome to Punkspider and IOStation,
3
00:00:04,380 --> 00:00:06,683
making a mess all over the internet.
4
00:00:07,600 --> 00:00:08,960
I am Jason Hopper,
5
00:00:08,960 --> 00:00:11,910
and I'm the Director
of Research at QOMPLX,
6
00:00:11,910 --> 00:00:13,083
and I'm here with-
7
00:00:14,000 --> 00:00:15,150
- I'm Alejandro Caceres.
8
00:00:15,150 --> 00:00:19,280
I'm the Director of Computer
Network Exploitation at QOMPLX.
9
00:00:19,280 --> 00:00:21,910
- Years ago, Alex invented or developed
10
00:00:21,910 --> 00:00:23,710
a system called PunkSPIDER,
11
00:00:23,710 --> 00:00:26,930
and I developed something
called IOStation.
12
00:00:26,930 --> 00:00:28,940
They're both pretty cool tools,
13
00:00:28,940 --> 00:00:30,860
and we've been dusting them off lately
14
00:00:30,860 --> 00:00:32,460
and starting to find some really good ways
15
00:00:32,460 --> 00:00:33,860
that we can work together.
16
00:00:33,860 --> 00:00:37,210
And this talk is just kind
of about how they started,
17
00:00:37,210 --> 00:00:38,700
you know, how they're going
18
00:00:38,700 --> 00:00:40,513
and where they're gonna be soon.
19
00:00:41,710 --> 00:00:44,830
- Yeah, so start off with
a little history lesson
20
00:00:44,830 --> 00:00:47,880
on what the fuck is PunkSPIDER, right?
21
00:00:47,880 --> 00:00:51,830
So PunkSPIDER was a distributed
math web application

00:00:51,830 --> 00:00:54,460
fuzzing project run over a Hadoop cluster

00:00:54,460 --> 00:00:56,860
and storage in a distributed backend.

00:00:56,860 --> 00:00:58,640
Don't worry if you didn't
fully understand that

00:00:58,640 --> 00:01:00,860
we'll be going through
what the fuck that means

00:01:00,860 --> 00:01:02,623
in a few later slides.

00:01:03,500 --> 00:01:06,060
It was based on some older technology.
28
00:01:06,060 --> 00:01:09,620
You vaguely might remember
it as that showed anything

00:01:09,620 --> 00:01:12,600
with some SQL injection or
some other vulnerabilities

00:01:12,600 --> 00:01:15,020
about like websites or some shit,

00:01:15,020 --> 00:01:17,550
that's usually how people remember it.
32
00:01:17,550 --> 00:01:19,720
So if you remember something like that,

00:01:19,720 --> 00:01:20,553
that was QOMPLX.

00:01:21,420 --> 00:01:23,700
It was presented at ShmooCon on 2013,
35
00:01:23,700 --> 00:01:27,210
and also at the psych guest appearance
36
00:01:27,210 --> 00:01:29,713
at the DEFCON 2014 as well, so.
37
00:01:30,660 --> 00:01:33,310
Still a long time ago
during this old release,

everything was MapReduced, right?

00:01:35,510 --> 00:01:37,660
If you remember that time
of where big technology

was the big buzz word,

instead of fucking like
blockchain or whatever,

then you remember times
